title: Flipped classroom improves student learning in health professions education: a meta-analysis
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether the flipped classroom approach improves student learning compared with traditional classroom instruction in health professions education. The authors note that flipped classrooms had become increasingly popular, but evidence on learning outcomes had not yet been synthesized in a meta-analysis focused specifically on objective achievement measures.

The intervention studied was a flipped classroom model in which students reviewed pre-recorded instructional videos before face-to-face class meetings, and in-class time was used for active learning activities such as quizzes, discussion, and problem solving. The review excluded studies that relied only on reading materials, online-only courses without face-to-face meetings, or designs without a comparable traditional classroom condition. The included studies covered medical students, pharmacy students, nursing students, public health students, dental students, chiropractic students, and other health professions learners across multiple countries, with most studies using historical control designs and a smaller number using quasi-experimental or randomized designs.

Across 28 comparative studies involving 4,715 students, the meta-analysis found a significant overall benefit for flipped classrooms over traditional instruction on student learning outcomes. The effect was modest but reliable, and results did not meaningfully differ by research design, student type, or whether pre-class readings or exercises were provided. The strongest moderator finding was that flipped classrooms were more effective when instructors began in-class sessions with quizzes on the pre-class materials. The authors also found that most surveyed students preferred the flipped format, though they noted limitations such as inconsistent reporting of instructional details and a lack of long-term retention data.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis with a clearly described search strategy, inclusion criteria, effect-size synthesis, moderator analyses, and publication-bias checks. Although the primary studies vary in design quality and are mostly historical controls, the review itself is a high-level evidence synthesis.
impact_tier_rationale: The pooled learning effect is medium in size (SMD=0.33), exceeding the threshold for blue impact. The findings are positive and fairly robust across subgroups, indicating a meaningful effect on student learning in the studied population.

interventions.use_case: flipped classroom instruction using pre-recorded video lectures before face-to-face sessions, with in-class active learning and quizzes in health professions education

finding.finding_summary: Across 28 comparative studies (n=2295 flipped; n=2420 traditional), the flipped classroom produced a statistically significant improvement in student learning performance versus traditional instruction. The pooled standardized mean difference was SMD=0.33 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.46, p<0.001), based on objective post-tests/exams in health professions education.
finding.measure: Objective student learning performance on post-tests, exams, and similar objective assessments

finding.finding_summary: Learner perception and preference favored the flipped classroom: in five survey-based studies, 228 of 320 respondents (71%) preferred flipped over traditional classrooms. The meta-analysis also reports that more respondents preferred flipped classes, suggesting higher satisfaction/engagement even though this was not the primary outcome.
